scenario: AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. Scenario:
AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She also has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can not afford it. This was confirmed by both the bully, and the friend. My daughter was silent on the way home and i informed her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get you in a lot of trouble. and that in the future she needs to speak to myself or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost her shit on me, in full tears, telling me that this is a one way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn’t want us to intervene. I am wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: I would rate this as 1, meaning YTA (You're The Asshole). Calling the police on your daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing was an extreme and misguided approach. While it's understandable that you wanted to address the issue of missing money, involving law enforcement and humiliating your daughter in front of her peers was not an appropriate or effective way to handle the situation. Instead of teaching your daughter a lesson, you may have inadvertently caused her more harm and trauma. By pulling her out of class and involving the police, you put her in a situation where she felt embarrassed, scared, and potentially vulnerable to retaliation from the bully. It's also concerning that you didn't consider the possibility that there might be a valid reason for your daughter's actions, such as being bullied or trying to help a friend in need. Your approach assumed that she was simply stealing for personal gain, without taking into account the complexities of the situation. Your wife's reaction and your daughter's concerns about retaliation and losing her friend suggest that your actions may have caused long-term damage to your relationship with your daughter and potentially put her in a more difficult situation. A more constructive approach would have been to have an open and honest conversation with your daughter, asking her why she took the money and listening to her perspective. This would have allowed you to address the issue in a more empathetic and supportive way, rather than resorting to punitive measures that may have caused more harm than good.
